To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca2+ has two actions at the ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells: it stimulates recruitment of reserve vesicles to a releasable pool and refills the releasable pool from the reserve pool.

the capacity of the reserve vesicle pool is similar to the total number of vesicles at the synapse, and that Ca2+ stimulates refilling of the releasable vesicle pool and recruitment of vesicles from cytoplasm to reserve pool.
calcium regulates the supply of vesicles at ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying neurotransmitter release from the ribbon synapse.
the mechanisms by which Ca2+ regulates exocytosis.
the mechanisms of exocytotic secretion at the synapse of bipolar cells in the vertebrate retina.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Ca2+ concentration in the vicinity of the ribbon synapse is regulated by Ca2+-binding proteins and that this Ca2+ concentration regulates both the rate and extent of exocytotic release.
Ca2+ has two actions that can be differentiated by introduction to the Ca2+-chelator EGta.

the Ca2+ concentration regulates the supply of vesicles in two ways: one action stimulates the refilling of the reserve pool from the cytoplamic vesicles and the second action recruits vesicles to the ribbon synapses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ is the main regulator of synaptic transmission at ribbon synapses.
the ribbon is a site of Ca2+ regulation of exocytotic supply.
Ca2+ stimulates vesicle recycling and replenishment of releasable pools in the ribbon synapse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ is involved in regulating vesicle supply to the release site.
the supply of releable vesicles is regulated by Ca2+ at the ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells.
Ca2+ can regulate both the release and the replenishment of vesicles at the synapse.
